implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent.atomic provides AtomicInteger, AtomicReference, AtomicLong and the CAS-based updaters, and Java 9 added VarHandle, which is the general-purpose answer: a VarHandle gives atomic access to any field, including one inside an object, with explicit memory-order modes (plain, opaque, acquireRelease, volatile). VarHandle is the right tool when the atomic is a field of an existing object rather than a dedicated AtomicInteger - it avoids the extra indirection and the wrapper object. Java's memory model is the same release/acquire framework; volatile gives sequential consistency, and AtomicInteger's methods are volatile in the JMM sense, which is stronger than acquire-release and costs a full fence on some architectures.
idiom_name: java.util.concurrent.atomic.* and java.lang.invoke.VarHandle for field-level atomics
pitfalls: AtomicInteger and its siblings are volatile in the JMM sense, which is stronger than acquire-release and compiles to a full fence on ARM - a hot counter using them pays more than VarHandle's setRelease/compareAndExchange.
VarHandle access modes are a long list and easy to misuse: plain gives atomicity with NO ordering at all, which is a data race waiting to happen.

AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater and AtomicLongFieldUpdater are the older alternative to VarHandle and work only on fields the updater is told about; a mismatch between the updater's type and the field's type is a runtime error.
A field declared volatile is atomic but not indivisible: volatile count++ is still a read-modify-write race, and AtomicInteger's incrementAndGet is not.
